There's obviously lots of ways you could do this, especially if you wanna get efficent about this, but I'm lazy: I made a sample file of your data called "junk":

curomo@localhost$ cat junk ~~~ (xxx) xxx xxxx Jul 3, 2016 08:48:41 146xxxxxx1786 1 (body of message 1v here), 1 ~~~ (xxx) xxx xxxx Jul 4, 2016 08:50:41 146xxxxxx1786 1 (body of message 2 here), 1 ~~~ (xxx) xxx xxxx Jul 5, 2016 08:52:41 146xxxxxx1786 1 (body of message 4 here), 1 ~~~ (xxx) xxx xxxx Jul 6, 2016 08:54:41 146xxxxxx1786 1 (body of message 3456 gfd jhere), 1 ~~~ (xxx) xxx xxxx Jul 8, 2016 08:55:41 146xxxxxx1786 1 (body of message cw vc2e c 2 v4 here), 1 [2016-07-03 21:29.22] curomo@localhost$ cat junk | cut -d " " -f2-8,11- | rev | cut -d" " -f 2- | rev | sed s/,$//g (xxx) xxx xxxx Jul 3, 2016 08:48:41 (body of message 1v here) (xxx) xxx xxxx Jul 4, 2016 08:50:41 (body of message 2 here) (xxx) xxx xxxx Jul 5, 2016 08:52:41 (body of message 4 here) (xxx) xxx xxxx Jul 6, 2016 08:54:41 (body of message 3456 gfd jhere) (xxx) xxx xxxx Jul 8, 2016 08:55:41 (body of message cw vc2e c 2 v4 here) to break that down:

cat = sends the file to the standard out

| = reads from std out

cut -d " " -f2-8,11- = means using space as the delimiter for fields, print out fields 2 thru 8 and 11 until the end of the line

rev = reverse the order of characters in the line, when i don't know how many fields there are and I want to remove the nth from the end, this let's me count backwards.

cut -d " " -f 2- - this basically removed this first field in the line, which would be the last if the line was forward

rev = make it foward again

sed s/,$//g = any string that ends in a comma, remove the comma

This would all be much cleaner and faster with just pure awk, but like I said, I'm lazy and awk syntax takes thinking.
